ATM (Asynchronous Transfer Mode) is a layer 2 protocol, bit-oriented. In earlier protocols the PDU was of variable length; in ATM it is of fixed length and so small that it is called a cell: 53 bytes.

With variable-length frames the equipment has to wait for each frame to be complete, and each one takes a different time. With all PDUs equal, the switching time can be predicted and bounded: fixed, small delay, low latency.

It is also connection-oriented, lets you define quality of service for each connection, and handles bandwidth on demand.
It was designed to reach end to end, but users stayed with Ethernet: ATM remained in the provider's network.
Each cell is 53 bytes: 5 of header + 48 of data. The switch takes the same time to process any of them.
The cell header, in UNI and in NNI

There are two interfaces: UNI (User to Network Interface), which we use to connect to an ATM switch, and NNI (Network to Network Interface), which joins two nodes. The header changes only slightly from one to the other.

  • GFC (Generic Flow Control): only in UNI, because flow control is done between the user and the network.
  • VPI and VCI: together they identify the connection, like the DLCI in Frame Relay.
  • Payload Type: type of payload (user cell or OAM) and congestion indication.
  • CLP: cell priority. When 1, it can be dropped, just like the DE bit.
  • HEC: header error control.
Five bytes of header for 48 of data: ATM has more overhead than the earlier protocols.

The HEC is 1 byte that checks the other 4: it detects errors in the header and corrects up to 1 bit. ATM does not check errors on the data field. The network sets CLP = 1 when the user exceeds some traffic parameter.

The identifier has two parts because connections were designed with a hierarchy: virtual channels (VC) travel grouped within virtual paths (VP).

  • A VP switch switches paths: it changes the VPI and the channels inside follow it without anyone touching their VCI. With a single change the provider re-routes all the connections of that path.
  • A VC switch switches channels: since the channel lies inside a path, it switches both the VPI and the VCI.

An end-to-end connection (VCC) thus goes through different paths along the way.
Grouping channels into paths lets the provider manage its customers' traffic more efficiently.

ATM is connection-oriented: one end requests a VCC through a signaling protocol, indicating whom it wants to connect to and what characteristics the connection will have.

  • The switch checks whether a path (VPC) exists to the destination. If it does not exist, it creates it.
  • Then it checks whether that path satisfies the QoS, that is, whether the network has the resources requested. If it does, it makes the connection.
  • If not, it asks the user to modify the request: the user can accept, and it is connected, or the request is rejected.
The connection is established only if the network can meet the requested quality of service.
VCCs can be user – user (they carry data end to end), user – network (signaling), or network – network (routing information between switches).

The HEC is computed with a procedure similar to HDLC's and allows correcting 1 erroneous bit in the header.

Once the connection is established, the node checks it cell after cell:

  • By default it is in correction mode. As long as no cell has errors, it stays there.
  • If it detects an error in a header it switches to detection mode: a single erroneous bit is corrected; if there are several, the cell is dropped.
  • In detection mode, if the next cell arrives without error it goes back to correction; if the HEC is erroneous again, the cell is dropped.
An isolated bit is corrected; if errors repeat, the problem is assumed to be something else.
No error: stays in correction mode, with no action.
Another error: the cell is dropped and it stays in detection mode.

The physical layer has to delimit the cells, and here there is no flag: synchronization is obtained with the HEC.

  • HUNT (capture): the receiver takes a cell-sized block and computes the HEC. If it is incorrect, it shifts one bit and computes again.
  • PRESYNC: a correct HEC can be a cell or a coincidence. It advances cell by cell: if the next one fails, it goes back to HUNT.
  • SYNC: after several consecutive correct cells it knows where each one starts and ends, and processes them one at a time. If a series of cells with errors appears, it has lost synchronization and goes back to HUNT.
The same byte serves two purposes: protecting the header and marking where each cell starts.
The physical layer also monitors errors, inserts idle cells when there is no data, and maintains synchronization.
In SYNC the previous diagram applies: an isolated bit is corrected and the cell is processed.
AAL: adapting what comes from above

Above the physical layer (generally SDH), ATM is divided in two: the ATM layer proper and the AAL, the adaptation layer.

The upper layer wants to transmit, for example, a 1500-byte IP datagram, and a cell holds 48. The AAL hides that characteristic with two sublayers:

  • Convergence: adds auxiliary bytes to the PDU.
  • Segmentation and reassembly: cuts it into 48-byte blocks, which fit in the cell's data field.

It also deals with transmission errors, lost or misinserted cells, and flow control.
It is not fragmented at the IP level: it is segmented in the AAL and everything is transmitted at once.

If it were fragmented by IP using 48 bytes as the MTU, each fragment would repeat the 20 bytes of IP header and carry only 28 of data. With segmentation, the IP header travels in a single block and the rest are parts of the datagram: 1500 / 48 gives about 32 cells (H = 5-byte ATM header).

Every kind of service can be transmitted over ATM, not just data. There are four classes, each with its AAL:

  • A: constant bit rate, with source–destination timing. AAL1.
  • B: the same, but with variable rate. AAL2.
  • C: connection-oriented data. AAL5.
  • D: connectionless data. AAL3/4.

Depending on the AAL, convergence adds the necessary auxiliary information (timestamp, error detection…) to recover the signal exactly as it came in.

When requesting a connection, the user indicates which service category is needed.
ATM Forum categories. Real time: CBR (constant bit rate) and VBR (variable), equivalent to classes A and B. Non-real time: VBR, ABR (available bit rate), and UBR (unspecified bit rate).
Traffic descriptor, QoS, CAC, and UPC

Along with the category, when requesting a VCC the user supplies a traffic descriptor (what it is going to transmit) and the QoS parameters (what it expects from the network), for both directions.

Call Admission Control is the network's signaling function: based on all those values, it accepts or not the connection.

Once the connection is established, the switch runs UPC (User Parameter Control): it compares what the user sends against what was requested and checks that the contracted PCR and SCR are respected. It is the same thing the Frame Relay node did when it counted bits so that we would not exceed the CIR.
CAC decides before connecting; UPC watches while the connection lasts.
What is asked of the network

• Cells of 53 bytes (5 + 48): predictable switching time and low latency.
  • Connection-oriented: each one is identified by VPI / VCI, channels within paths.
  • The HEC protects the header, corrects 1 bit, and also delimits cells (HUNT → PRESYNC → SYNC).
  • The AAL adapts each service: convergence plus segmentation into 48-byte blocks.
  • Quality of service per connection: category, traffic descriptor, and QoS. CAC admits, UPC polices.
